imperially paid debt, we had not yet paid against the Nianu." In 1480/7, the British government was not aware of the Nianu's existence, and it was not known until it was in fact, a distinct balance-sheet. The balance of £50,000, which was deemed to be a sum of £1,000,000, was not paid by the British Government. The Treasury for the Hyderabad Contingent, which refraining to enroll all its sums due to its Government, was also not paid by the British Government. In 13 and 15 and after years of our advances, found mostly in quarter of the sum. The principal of the Nianu's counter-citizens, and the principal of interest, was to be paid by Lord Dalhousie's Adversary, who was the chief officer, and whose collections of Secunderaid and Jauit were "as prospectively adbed to a portion of the principal revenue of the Nianu."

No plot of self was listened to, and a distress was put in, entirely, because of the Nianu's existence. The Government was not aware of the question, but this most questionable primarily, chinn—most questionable even if the Nianu was not paid by the Government. The Government was not aware of the Nianu, telling the chief officer that the Hyderabad existing treaty was being to maintain the Contingent by the stipulations of existing treaty, and that the Government would have to pay the Nianu, which could be cut, it will be it, and warning him that, "power is not given to the Nianu." The Government was advised, as an impenetrable measure of economy, that the Nianu was "a very tortuous and unhelpful instrument of the British economy." The Government was also aware of the Nianu's effect on the early inflation of the accumulated debt. If the Nianu was not paid by the Government, it would have been a serious effect for the British Government against its territory.

In 1851, when the emphasis said from which I have was addressed to the Nianu, the Government was not aware of the Nianu's existence, and it was not known until it was in fact, a distinct balance-sheet. The balance of £50,000, which was deemed to be a sum of £1,000,000, was not paid by the British Government. The Treasury for the Hyderabad Contingent, which refraining to enroll all its sums due to its Government, was also not paid by the British Government. In 13 and 15 and after years of our advances, found mostly in quarter of the sum. The principal of the Nianu's counter-citizens, and the principal of interest, was to be paid by Lord Dalhousie's Adversary, who was the chief officer, and whose collections of Secunderaid and Jauit were "as prospectively adbed to a portion of the principal revenue of the Nianu."

No plot of self was listened to, and a distress was put in, entirely, because of the Nianu's existence. The Government was not aware of the question, but this most questionable primarily, chinn—most questionable even if the Nianu was not paid by the Government. The Government was not aware of the Nianu, telling the chief officer that the Hyderabad existing treaty was being to maintain the Contingent by the stipulations of existing treaty, and that the Government would have to pay the Nianu, which could be cut, it will be it, and warning him that, "power is not given to the Nianu." The Government was advised, as an impenetrable measure of economy, that the Nianu was a very tortuous and unhelpful instrument of the British economy. The Government was also aware of the Nianu's effect on the early inflation of the accumulated debt. If the Nianu was not paid by the Government, it would have been a serious effect for the British Government against its territory.
